title: This 300-Year-Old Shipwreck Wood Became Two Beautiful Dresses
summary:
What would you do with wood from a 300-year-old shipwreck? Most people would put it in a museum. But a team in Finland had a wild idea: turn it into fashion. They made two elegant, floor-length dresses from the ancient wood. And they look amazing.

The wood came from the "Hahtiperä wreck," a cargo ship from the 1600s. Its remains were found under a hotel parking lot in Oulu, Finland, during a 2019 renovation. Archeologists saved the main hull, but some wet wood was too damaged. Instead of tossing it, the Finnish Heritage Agency asked Aalto University to give it a second life.

Researchers there had already made sustainable textile fibers from paper and cardboard. They used the same eco-friendly process, called the "Ioncell method," on the old wood. First, they cut it into small pieces and shaved off centuries of dirt. Then they shredded the clean wood into pulp and mixed it with a non-toxic salt-based solvent. The mixture was spun into strong, smooth yarn.

Wood contains cellulose—the same natural material in cotton and linen. So the new fiber was strong. In fact, scientists said it felt like silk and was stronger than cotton. To honor the ship's history, they didn't use dye or bleach. The yarn kept its natural tan-brown color and a slight shine.

Textile designer Anna-Mari Leppisaari created a pattern inspired by wood grain and computer pixels. An industrial knitting machine turned the yarn into two identical, seamless dresses—with no waste. One dress is on display at the Oulu Art Museum through September 2026. The other will be shown at Aalto University from September to October 2026. As researcher Pirjo Kääriäinen said, "If something this beautiful can be made from centuries-old wood, why do we keep throwing away materials that could still be reused?"
why_it_matters: It shows that things we throw away — old wood, old clothes — can become something new, a way of thinking you can use at home now and in whatever job you do later.

background_read: Oulu is a city in northern Finland, a country in northern Europe where winters are long and cold.
A shipwreck is what is left of a ship after it sinks; old wrecks often get buried in mud, which helps keep the wood from rotting away.

Aalto University is a school in Finland where scientists study new materials — researchers there developed the Ioncell method to make cloth out of wood instead of oil, and today huge amounts of old clothes end up as trash, so new ways to reuse materials really matter.
Article_Structure: WHO: Researchers at Aalto University, the Finnish Heritage Agency, and textile designer Anna-Mari Leppisaari.
WHAT: They turned wood from a 300-year-old shipwreck into strong yarn and knitted two floor-length dresses.
WHERE: Oulu, Finland — the wreck was found under a hotel parking lot, and the dresses are shown at the Oulu Art Museum and Aalto University.
WHY: To prove that old materials can be given a second life instead of being thrown away, using an eco-friendly method with no dye or bleach.

perspectives.description: They get to see history and fashion mixed together, and the dresses help people imagine the old ship and its story.
They might worry that turning part of an old shipwreck into dresses uses up material that should be kept safe for study.
They are excited because the same method could turn old clothes and waste wood into new fabric instead of letting it pile up in landfills.
